comparison: Both address the CheA interactor identification (C46-C50). OpenEval finds the multi-tiered validation approach provides strong evidence with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers express concern about the large number of interactors and question physiological relevance, marking this as UNCERTAIN rather than SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate domain mapping data (C5, C58-C62). OpenEval finds the domain mapping experiments sound and well-supported. Peer reviewers acknowledge the interaction data but raise fundamental concerns about protein identity, questioning whether PP_2969 is truly a copper-responsive CsoR (noting it's linked to Ni/Co resistance), marking this UNCERTAIN.

OpenEval evaluates phosphorylation inhibition and chemotaxis effects (C6, C51, C53-C54, C56-C57) as SUPPORTED with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers group these claims with domain mapping data and express uncertainty about the protein's identity and metal specificity, which undermines interpretation of functional effects.

Both address negative control experiments (C56-C57, C52). OpenEval finds these controls appropriately rule out alternative mechanisms. Peer reviewers explicitly SUPPORT these negative findings, which help establish the inhibition mechanism doesn't involve phosphotransfer or ATPase activity.

Both evaluate copper-dependent modulation of chemotaxis (C7, C89-C91). OpenEval finds genetic and biochemical evidence converge effectively. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN, questioning physiological relevance of copper-dependent effects given fundamental concerns about protein identity and metal specificity.

Both address metal-binding data (C63-C66). OpenEval finds MST assays provide quantitative binding constants with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers explicitly reject this as UNSUPPORTED, stating Cu(II) binding follows Irving-Williams series and is not physiologically relevant, noting true CsoR proteins respond to Cu(I) with affinities of 10^-18 M determined by competition assays.

Both evaluate DNA-binding and gene expression data (C10-C11, C67-C69, C72-C73). OpenEval acknowledges modest regulatory effects and appropriate discussion of limitations. Peer reviewers mark this UNSUPPORTED, stating protein concentrations exceed physiological ranges, wrong DNA target was used (should be PP_2970 not copA genes), and binding is likely non-specific.

Both address copper-dependent weakening of CheA-CsoR interaction (C8, C79-C82). OpenEval finds convergence of MST and pull-down methods strengthens conclusions. Peer reviewers mark this UNCERTAIN, questioning physiological relevance of reported affinities and how specific responses occur with heterogeneous CheA-complexes.

Both evaluate point mutation analysis (C83, C85-C86, C88). OpenEval finds mutagenesis effectively identifies critical residue C69. Peer reviewers group this with other copper-dependent modulation data and mark UNCERTAIN due to fundamental concerns about protein identity as copper-responsive regulator.

OpenEval addresses C83 (CsoRC69A reduced copper binding) as part of mutation analysis. Peer reviewers' rejection of metal-binding data as UNSUPPORTED applies here, as they state Cu(II) binding measurements are not physiologically relevant for CsoR proteins.

Both evaluate chemotaxis behavioral assays (C13, C92-C98). OpenEval finds multiple complementary assays demonstrate copper chemorepellence with CheA-dependence well-established. Peer reviewers mark UNCERTAIN, questioning how putative CheA interactions integrate into diverse chemotaxis responses and noting the study is incomplete without additional experiments.

Both address quantitative cell tracking data (C14, C99-C102). OpenEval finds single-cell tracking provides robust evidence distinguishing CsoR's role in direction from CheA's role in motility. Peer reviewers mark UNCERTAIN, with concerns about model integration and fundamental uncertainty about protein's metal specificity undermining mechanistic interpretation.

Both evaluate cross-species interaction data (C15, C103-C106). OpenEval notes interactions in 4 of 7 species but acknowledges untested functional significance limits conclusions. Peer reviewers mark UNCERTAIN, noting concerns about two-hybrid methodology (long growth time, solid plate Miller unit determination) and that CsoR proteins are typically found only in gram-positive bacteria.

Both address PhaD characterization (C52, C55). OpenEval finds parallel characterization provides internal validation. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the negative control findings (C52) showing no phosphotransfer, though they don't specifically comment on PhaD's inhibitory activity.

OpenEval evaluates EMSA with DTT and metal specificity (C74-C77) as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers' UNSUPPORTED evaluation of metal-binding data applies here, as they reject Cu(II) measurements as physiologically irrelevant and state true CsoR proteins respond to Cu(I).

OpenEval addresses EMSA metal specificity (C74, C76-C77). Peer reviewers' UNSUPPORTED evaluation of DNA-binding experiments applies, stating assays use non-physiological protein concentrations and wrong DNA targets, resulting in non-specific binding.

Both evaluate growth assays showing no copper resistance phenotype (C78, C70). OpenEval finds these negative results are important controls showing CheA-CsoR interaction affects chemotaxis rather than copper resistance. Peer reviewers SUPPORT this finding, consistent with their argument that CueR and CopR are the primary copper resistance regulators.

OpenEval addresses gene expression data (C70) showing cheA deletion has no effect on copper-resistance genes. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their UNSUPPORTED evaluation of regulatory claims, noting lack of effect on copA gene expression is consistent with CueR (not CsoR) being the regulator.

OpenEval evaluates broader metal-responsive regulatory functions (C71) as SUPPORTED but notes untested functional significance. Peer reviewers' UNSUPPORTED evaluation of DNA-binding and gene regulation applies here, given their concerns about non-specific binding and wrong regulatory targets.

Both address copper relief of CsoR inhibition (C9, C87). OpenEval finds convergence of biochemical and behavioral evidence supports the regulatory mechanism. Peer reviewers mark related claims UNCERTAIN due to fundamental concerns about protein identity and physiological relevance of copper-dependent modulation.

Both evaluate the proposed regulatory model (C107-C110). OpenEval finds the model largely supported though some aspects are inferred. Peer reviewers explicitly state the data does NOT support the model (UNSUPPORTED), emphasizing PP_2969 is linked to Ni/Co (not Cu) resistance and results are inconsistent with published CsoR properties.

OpenEval evaluates structural comparison between CsoR and PhaD (C119-C120) showing no similarity, suggesting convergent evolution. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval evaluates BTH assays showing point-mutated CsoRs maintain CheA interaction (C84), establishing distinct copper-binding and CheA-binding sites. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.
